_meta: Two independent measurements of the same quantity, one precise and one noisy, each with its own known uncertainty, used to show that combining measurements by a simple average is not just suboptimal but can be worse than using the precise measurement alone -- and that the right combination weights each measurement by its precision (inverse variance). When you have several independent measurements of one true value, each with a standard deviation, the instinct is to average them: add the values, divide by the count. That treats a measurement good to a tenth of a unit and a measurement good to five units as equals, so the noisy one drags the average around, and the variance of the simple average is the average of the variances scaled down only by the count -- which, when one measurement is much noisier, stays large. In fact a simple average of a precise measurement and a noisy one has a larger variance than the precise measurement by itself: averaging in the bad data degraded your best data. The minimum-variance unbiased combination instead weights each measurement by one over its variance (inverse-variance, or precision, weighting): the precise measurement gets most of the weight, the noisy one a little, and the combined variance is one over the sum of the inverse variances -- smaller than any single measurement, including the best one. true_value is the quantity being measured (used only to show which estimate lands closer); measurements each give an observed value and its sigma. The simple and inverse-variance-weighted estimates, their variances, and the weights are computed. Stdlib only.
